questions.prompt: Put these steps of the Procure-to-Pay (P2P) cycle, per Lesson 2, in the correct order.
items: Requisition: an employee requests that the steel be purchased
Purchase Order (PO): Procurement approves the requisition and issues a PO to the supplier
Receipt: the steel arrives and a receiving clerk records it
Invoice: the supplier's invoice is matched against the PO and the receipt (three-way match)
Payment: Accounts Payable pays the supplier, posting to the General Ledger
questions.explain: Procure-to-Pay always runs Requisition (a request, not yet a commitment) to Purchase Order (now a legal commitment) to Receipt (goods arrive) to Invoice (matched against the PO and receipt via the three-way match) to Payment (which finally posts to the General Ledger). Skipping or reordering any step breaks the control the three-way match exists to provide.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the one place where a transaction's details are considered authoritative — the single source of truth the company actually uses — is called its ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 1 defines the system of record as the single authoritative source for a piece of business data. If the ERP says a customer owes $4,200, that is the number the company uses, not whatever a spreadsheet on someone's laptop might say.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Order-to-Cash (O2C) and process flow in general, per Lesson 2.
options: Every business process, whatever module it starts in, eventually produces an accounting entry that lands in the General Ledger
In Order-to-Cash, the customer invoice is generated before the warehouse ships the goods, not after
The three-way match compares a purchase order, a receipt, and a supplier invoice before approving payment
A new consultant should learn Oracle Fusion screen by screen first, then infer the underlying business process later
Order-to-Cash's final step posts the sale, the cost of goods, and the cash received automatically to the General Ledger
questions.explain: Both P2P and O2C eventually feed the General Ledger, which is exactly the pattern Lesson 2 asks you to internalize. The three-way match is a real control described in the P2P walkthrough. O2C's accounting entries post automatically at the end of the cycle. Order-to-Cash actually generates the invoice from what was shipped, after fulfillment, not before it — and Lesson 2 explicitly says learning screen by screen first is backwards; process understanding should come first.

questions.prompt: Blue Harbor Manufacturing's Procurement team updates a supplier's banking details once, inside Procurement. When Accounts Payable later pays that same supplier, it automatically uses the updated details, with nobody re-entering anything in Payables. What does this illustrate, per Lesson 3?
options: Master data — the supplier record is a shared reference record used by both Procurement and Payables, not a separate copy each module keeps for itself
The three-way match, which automatically propagates banking details whenever a PO is approved
The General Ledger pushing supplier updates out to every other module that references that supplier
Procurement and Payables each keep their own separate copy of the supplier record, kept in sync by a nightly batch job
questions.explain: Lesson 3 describes master data — supplier, customer, employee records — as shared reference data used across modules rather than duplicated. The same supplier record used in Procurement is the one Accounts Payable pays, which is exactly why updating it once in Procurement is enough; there's no separate copy in Payables to keep in sync, with or without a batch job.

questions.prompt: Match each module family from Lesson 3 to what it actually covers.
right: Requisitions, purchase orders, supplier qualification, contracts, sourcing/negotiation
General Ledger, Accounts Payable, Accounts Receivable, Cash Management, Fixed Assets
Core HR records, compensation, benefits, payroll, talent management
questions.explain: Financials is the accounting core (GL, AP, AR, Cash, Fixed Assets). Procurement covers requisitions through sourcing. Supply Chain Management covers moving and making goods: inventory, order management, manufacturing, planning. HCM covers people: core HR, compensation, benefits, payroll, talent.

questions.prompt: What is Oracle Fusion Cloud Applications, per Lesson 6?
options: Oracle's modern, multi-tenant SaaS suite of business applications, built from the ground up to run on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, organized into pillars like ERP, SCM, HCM, CX, and EPM
Oracle's mature, on-premises ERP suite first released in the late 1990s
A single module inside Oracle E-Business Suite used only for financial reporting
A third-party reporting tool that connects to an Oracle database
Oracle's legacy on-premises database product line
A customization framework used to modify Oracle Fusion's underlying code
questions.explain: Lesson 6 defines Oracle Fusion Cloud Applications as Oracle's modern, multi-tenant SaaS suite built on OCI and organized into major pillars (ERP, SCM, HCM, CX, EPM), unified by a single shared data model — the strategic successor to older product lines Oracle acquired or built over the years.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes Oracle E-Business Suite, not Fusion Cloud — EBS is the mature, on-premises product first released in the late 1990s that Lesson 8 contrasts against Fusion Cloud. Confusing the two is exactly the mix-up Lesson 6 warns about: a lot of what you'll read online about 'Oracle ERP' is actually about an older product, not Fusion Cloud specifically.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Oracle Fusion Cloud runs on a ________ architecture, where many customer tenants share Oracle-managed infrastructure while their data stays securely isolated from each other.
questions.explain: Lesson 7 describes multi-tenant SaaS as many customers ('tenants') running on shared Oracle-managed infrastructure with isolated data, rather than each customer getting a dedicated copy of the hardware and software — what makes the economics of SaaS work in the first place.

questions.prompt: A company has run Oracle E-Business Suite for over a decade with heavy custom code, and is now also rolling out Oracle Fusion Cloud ERP for a newly acquired business unit, planning to run both for several years. What is this arrangement called, per Lesson 8?
options: Coexistence — running EBS and Fusion Cloud together, often during a gradual migration
Cutover — the specific window of activity right around go-live
Hypercare — a defined period of extra support staffing right after go-live
Fit-gap analysis — comparing business needs against standard system capability
questions.explain: Lesson 8 calls running EBS and Fusion Cloud side by side, often during a gradual migration, a coexistence strategy — exactly why EBS experience remains valuable in the job market even as new implementations increasingly choose Fusion Cloud.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Oracle's quarterly update cadence, per Lesson 10.
options: Oracle names each quarterly release using the last two digits of the year plus a letter, A through D
Every customer worldwide is updated on the exact same calendar day, regardless of cohort
A customer's non-production environment is typically updated a few weeks before production
Opt-in features turn on automatically the moment a quarterly update is applied
Reviewing readiness documentation and deciding on opt-in features is a recurring task, not a one-time implementation activity
questions.explain: Releases are named YYA through YYD. Cohorts (A, B, C) stagger which month within the quarter a customer is updated, so not everyone updates the same day. Non-production is deliberately updated before production, giving time to test. Opt-in features ship switched off, not enabled automatically — and reviewing readiness notes and opt-ins is a recurring quarterly habit, not a one-time implementation task.

questions.prompt: Put these events of a single quarterly update cycle, per Lesson 10, in the order they actually happen.
items: Oracle publishes "What's New" readiness documentation ahead of the release
The customer's non-production environment receives the quarterly update
The functional team tests critical business processes and decides which opt-in features to enable
The same update reaches the production environment a few weeks later
The functional team communicates the resulting changes to end users
questions.explain: Readiness documentation comes first so the team knows what's changing. The non-production environment is updated before production specifically to give time to test and decide on opt-ins. Only after that review does the same update reach production, and only then does it make sense to communicate the changes to the end users who will actually see them.

questions.prompt: Match each home page piece, per Lesson 11, to what it actually is.
right: The grid of work-area shortcut icons on the home page
A menu icon that opens the full list of work areas a user has access to
A small interactive widget surfacing glanceable, role-relevant information
The bar across the top of every page with search, notifications, and the account menu
questions.explain: The global header is the top bar present on every page with search, notifications, and the account menu. The Navigator is the menu icon opening the full list of accessible work areas. The springboard is the grid of shortcut icons on the home page itself. Infolets are the small widgets surfacing glanceable, role-relevant information.

questions.prompt: An AP clerk needs to see, every single day, the exact same list: all invoices over $5,000, still pending approval, for the Manufacturing business unit. Per Lesson 14, which tool lets that specific filter combination be remembered and re-run with one click, instead of being rebuilt from scratch each day?
options: A saved search
A Favorite
Global search
A Quick Action
questions.explain: Lesson 14 distinguishes a saved search — a stored set of filter criteria on a specific list, re-runnable with one click — from a Favorite, which is just a shortcut to a page, not a remembered filter. A saved search is exactly the tool for 'I always filter this list the same specific way.'

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: inside most work areas, a ________ panel lists the specific activities available there, often grouped by category — this is where a user actually starts doing something.
questions.explain: Lesson 13 describes the Tasks panel as the list of specific activities available inside a work area, often grouped by category, such as Journals, Period Close, and Allocations inside General Accounting — clicking a task there opens the page needed to actually perform it.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about scheduled processes, per Lesson 15.
options: A process stuck in Pending status is queued but has not yet started
Checking a job's status and log is usually the first troubleshooting step when a user reports that nothing happened
A scheduled process always blocks the user's screen until it finishes running
A status of Warning means the job completed but produced something worth reviewing, not that it necessarily failed
Scheduled processes can only ever be submitted to run immediately, never on a recurring schedule
questions.explain: Pending means queued but not yet started. Checking the Scheduled Processes work area for status and log is the standard first troubleshooting step. Warning means it completed, with something worth reviewing, distinct from an outright Error. Scheduled processes exist precisely so heavy operations run in the background instead of blocking the screen, and they can be scheduled to run repeatedly, not only submitted once.

questions.prompt: A company copies its Production data into its non-production environment to keep testing realistic, overwriting whatever test data was there. What is this operation called, and what should an implementation team plan around because of it, per Lesson 16?
options: An environment refresh — which can wipe out any in-progress configuration work in non-production that hasn't been migrated elsewhere
A cutover — which permanently retires the old legacy system in favor of the new one
An opt-in feature activation — which only ever affects new functionality, never existing data
A fit-gap analysis — which only identifies gaps and never actually moves any data
A cohort reassignment — which changes which month a customer receives its quarterly update
A hypercare period — which adds extra support staffing immediately after go-live
questions.explain: Lesson 16 calls copying Production's data into non-production an environment refresh, and warns that it's powerful but disruptive: any configuration work in progress in that non-production environment that hasn't been migrated elsewhere can be wiped out, so implementation teams plan around refresh schedules deliberately.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B, cutover, is a different implementation-vocabulary term entirely (defined in Lesson 17) — the window of activity right around go-live where a company switches from its old system to the new one. It has nothing to do with copying Production data into a test environment; conflating the two mixes up an environment-management operation with a go-live milestone.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of an AP clerk going from signing in to actually creating a journal entry in the Order-to-Cash's final home, the General Ledger, in the correct order, per Lessons 11 through 13.
items: Sign in and land on the home page
Open the Navigator and select the General Accounting work area
Land on the General Accounting work area's own page, with its Tasks panel visible
Expand the Tasks panel's Journals group and click Create Journal
questions.explain: This is the Navigator-to-Work-Area-to-Task hierarchy from Lesson 13 in action: sign in to the home page first, open the Navigator to reach the specific work area (General Accounting), land on that work area's own page where the Tasks panel is visible, and only then drill into the Tasks panel itself to reach a specific task like Create Journal.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: ________ is the phase where actual end users, not just the project team, test the configured system against real scenarios before go-live, formally signing off that it meets their needs.
questions.explain: Lesson 17 defines UAT (User Acceptance Testing) as the phase where actual end users test the configured system against real scenarios and formally sign off before go-live — distinct from a CRP, which is the project team's own structured walkthrough earlier in the project.

questions.prompt: A project team needs to configure "Manage Payment Terms" for a client's Financials rollout. Per Lesson 18's hierarchy, which level of Setup and Maintenance does "Manage Payment Terms" sit at?
options: Task — a specific configuration activity, inside the Payables functional area, itself inside the Financials offering
Offering — the broadest grouping of everything a company has subscribed to
Functional Area — a grouping of related configuration within an offering
Implementation project — a named, scoped, trackable set of configuration tasks
questions.explain: Lesson 18 uses exactly this example: "Manage Payment Terms" is a Task, sitting inside the Payables functional area, which itself sits inside the broader Financials offering — the narrowest, most specific level of the Offering to Functional Area to Task hierarchy.

questions.prompt: Match each term from Lesson 19 to which side of the functional/technical divide it belongs to.
left: Deciding how the Chart of Accounts should be structured
right: A technical consultant's tool for mass-loading data
A technical consultant's scripting tool for specific business rules
A functional consultant's decision about ledger structure, made through business-process knowledge
A functional consultant's reporting activity, done without writing code
questions.explain: FBDI and Groovy are both technical-consultant tools — mass data loads and business-rule scripting, respectively. Deciding how the Chart of Accounts should be structured and building OTBI reports are both functional-consultant activities, done through Setup and Maintenance and business-process knowledge rather than code.

questions.prompt: A student just finished Oracle Fusion Cloud and ERP Foundations and is excited to start practicing hands-on. Per Lesson 20, what should they do about their Oracle Fusion practice-environment subscription right now?
options: Wait — activate it only when they reach Enterprise Structures & Chart of Accounts, since the very next course, Accounting Fundamentals for Oracle Professionals, is also entirely conceptual and doesn't need it
Activate it immediately, since every course on this path requires hands-on Oracle access from the start
Activate it through LTV Academy's own subscription, since OracleERPGuide access is bundled with tuition
Skip it entirely, since no course anywhere on this path ever requires hands-on Oracle access
questions.explain: Lesson 20 is explicit: the practice-instance subscription from OracleERPGuide is sold for a fixed roughly three-month window, is not included in LTV Academy tuition, and should be activated only once the student reaches Enterprise Structures & Chart of Accounts — the first course where hands-on exercises actually begin — since both this course and the next one are entirely conceptual and need no Oracle access at all.
